newsitem.title: PERU: Peru government says no to rebel proposal on talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru government says no to rebel proposal on talks.

text.p: Peru said on Thursday it had rejected a proposal by Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages in Lima that the Guatemalan government take part in talks to end the 30-day stand-off.

"The Peruvian government does not accept the proposal that a representative of the Guatemalan government take part in the commission," Peruvian government negotiator Domingo Palermo told a news conference.

The government believed that efforts to bring the Central American country into the talks meant the rebels were suggesting a similarity between the situation in Peru and the recently-ended civil war in Guatemala. Leftist guerrillas there laid down arms in December after more than 30 years of fighting.
"With this suggestion the aim is to establish an analogy with a completely different reality," Palermo said.

The Peruvian government says the rebel hostage takers, who stormed the residence of the Japanese ambassador on Dec. 17 during a cocktail party, are "terrorists" who have no support among the population.
It rejects any comparison between Central American guerrilla conflicts of the 1980s and early 1990s and the Peruvian government's fight against leftist rebel groups.
The rebels had suggested on Wednesday that Guatemala and an unnamed European country join a "guarantor commission" proposed by the government to try to end the hostage crisis.
Both sides have agreed to the participation of representatives from the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Vatican.

Palermo also said visits by the Red Cross to imprisoned members of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) in Peruvian jails were being suspended "in order to avoid disturbing the process of talks". He did not explain how such visits had been affecting the negotiations.
Palermo said the government was evaluating the rest of the rebel proposal. He did not say whether the government would accept the participation of a European country in the talks.
The rebel leader in the residence, Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, tried to issue a statement by walkie-talkie immediately after Palermo's news conference.
Severe interference made his message virtually unintelligible, although he could be heard asking that the Red Cross visit imprisoned MRTA leader Victor Polay Campos.
Earlier, police had broken in on the frequency used by the rebels as journalists tried to talk to him, giving rise to suspicion among reporters that police were jamming Cerpa's transmission.

Witnesses earlier said two young women among the approximately 15 heavily-armed rebels could be seen at the windows of the besieged residence, waving to reporters, munching food and occasionally laughing together.
One unidentified hostage also briefly appeared and waved.

Before Palermo's news conference, several hundred street vendors marched to the residence, in the latest of several such demonstrations by labour and neighbourhood groups, to demand the freedom of the hostages.

The rebels are demanding the government free about 400 of their jailed MRTA colleagues. President Alberto Fujimori has flatly refused that demand but says he is prepared to let the rebels leave Peru if they lay down their arms and free all their hostages.

Cerpa said in a radio statement on Wednesday that the rebels would not kill any of their hostages but also warned that without tangible progress in negotiations the crisis was "being pushed towards a military end".
